title: The boundary invariant
sub: What holds for lo and hi at every step: closed and half-open intervals, lower_bound, ~index in Array.BinarySearch and Span
cards/0/body:
Binary Search (LeetCode #704). The array nums is sorted in ascending order, its numbers are distinct, n ≤ 10⁴. Return the index of target or −1 — in O(log n).

You met the algorithm itself in the first unit. This lesson is about why it is correct and how to get the boundaries right in every variant of it. Signals of binary search: the data is sorted or the answer is monotonic (“the least x such that…”), and the constraints demand O(log n) per query.

Every variant rests on an invariant — a statement about lo and hi that holds before each iteration. For the closed interval it reads: if target is in the array, it is in nums[lo..hi]. At the start this is true — the whole array is a candidate. Each step preserves it: if nums[mid] < target, then everything left of mid is smaller too (the array is sorted), and lo = mid + 1 throws away only what certainly does not matter. The second obligation is that the interval shrinks by at least one element, so the loop terminates. Once lo > hi there are no candidates left — the answer is −1.

The rule for any variant: state the invariant first, then write the conditions. Every + 1, − 1, < or <= follows from it rather than being tuned against tests.
cards/1/q: In the closed variant someone wrote else hi = mid instead of hi = mid − 1. What happens?
cards/1/options/0: On some inputs the loop never ends: with lo == hi and nums[mid] > target the interval stops shrinking
cards/1/options/1: Nothing serious: mid is already checked, there will be one extra iteration
cards/1/options/3: hi becomes −1, and nums[mid] goes out of bounds
cards/1/explain: The first obligation still holds: nums[mid] > target, so the answer is not to the right of mid. The second one is broken — the interval must shrink. Example: [5], target = 3. lo = hi = mid = 0, 5 > 3, hi = mid = 0 — and the state never changes. In the closed variant mid has been fully checked, so it is discarded: hi = mid − 1.
cards/1/wrong/1: It is not just one extra iteration: with lo == hi the new hi equals the old one, and the loop spins forever.
cards/1/wrong/2: mid is computed as lo + (hi − lo) / 2, and how hi is moved has no effect on that.
cards/1/wrong/3: hi cannot reach −1 here: hi = mid ≥ lo ≥ 0. The real trouble is that with lo == hi the interval stops shrinking.
cards/2/body:
Problems like “first occurrence”, “where to insert”, “how many numbers are less than x” look for a boundary, not an element. For them a half-open interval and a different invariant are more convenient.

lower_bound(x) is the first index where a[i] ≥ x, or n if there is none. Invariant: everything left of lo is less than x, everything from hi on is not less than x. Only the band [lo, hi) is unknown. At the start lo = 0, hi = n: both known parts are empty, so the statement holds. Step: if a[mid] < x, mid joins the smaller ones — lo = mid + 1; otherwise it joins the not-smaller ones — hi = mid (it may be the answer, hence no − 1). End: lo == hi, nothing is unknown, and lo is the boundary itself.

Why this is robust: mid < hi always, so a[mid] never leaves the array, and both branches strictly shrink the band. One comparison per iteration and no equality check — which is why, with duplicates, you get the first occurrence.

upper_bound(x) is the first index where a[i] > x: the same code with <= instead of <. The two boundaries give you almost everything: x occurs upper − lower times, its last occurrence is at upper − 1, and the count of numbers in [L, R] is upper(R) − lower(L).
cards/3/q: Build upper_bound: the first index where a[i] > x.
cards/3/explain: The band [lo, hi) starts with hi = a.Length: if every element is ≤ x, the answer is n. The loop runs while the band is not empty: lo < hi. Elements equal to x go left together with the smaller ones — hence <=. In the else branch a[mid] > x, and mid may be the answer: hi = mid, no − 1.
cards/4/body:
.NET already has binary search: Array.BinarySearch and List<T>.BinarySearch. Inside is the closed variant with a three-way comparison, as at the start of the lesson. What it returns:

Found — the index. But with duplicates it is some of the equal ones: the documentation does not promise the first. Need the first — write lower_bound.
Not found — a negative number ~i, where i is the insertion point: the index of the first element greater than the value, or Length if there is none. That is lo when the loop exits. The closed variant actually guarantees a stronger statement: everything left of lo is less than target, everything right of hi is greater; when lo = hi + 1, the two parts meet exactly at the insertion point.

~i is bitwise NOT, equal to −i − 1. Plain −i would not do: insertion point 0 would give 0, indistinguishable from “found at index 0”. The same ~ converts it back.

Details: the (array, index, length, value) overload takes a length, not an end; the array must be sorted with the same comparer, otherwise the answer is meaningless, and there is no exception. Inserting into a sorted List: the search is O(log n), but Insert shifts the tail — O(n).

In a game: level from experience. Level thresholds are sorted, and the level is the last threshold not greater than xp, that is upper_bound(xp) − 1. With Array.BinarySearch: the index if xp hit a threshold exactly, otherwise the insertion point minus one.
cards/4/code:
int[] xp = { 0, 100, 250, 500, 1000 };   // threshold of each level
int i = Array.BinarySearch(xp, 300);       // -4: absent, insertion point ~(-4) = 3
int level = i >= 0 ? i : ~i - 1;           // 2: 250 reached, 500 not yet

var sorted = new List<int> { 1, 4, 9 };
int j = sorted.BinarySearch(5);            // -3: insert at index 2
sorted.Insert(j >= 0 ? j : ~j, 5);         // [1, 4, 5, 9]
cards/5/q: a = [10, 20, 30, 40]. Which statements about Array.BinarySearch(a, x) are true? Select all.
cards/5/options/4: On [10, 20, 20, 20, 30] with x = 20 it returns 1, the first occurrence
cards/5/explain: Not found means ~(insertion point). 5 is smaller than everything: point 0, ~0 = −1. 25 goes before 30, at index 2: ~2 = −3, while −2 would be ~1. 50 is greater than everything: point 4 = Length, ~4 = −5. With duplicates the first occurrence is not promised: in [10, 20, 20, 20, 30] the very first midpoint is index 2, it holds 20, and the method returns 2.
cards/6/body:
Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T> get the MemoryExtensions.BinarySearch extension methods — since .NET Core 2.1 and in .NET Standard 2.1, which means in Unity 2021.2+ as well. Same convention: the index or ~insertion point, but relative to the start of the slice. A slice AsSpan(start, length) copies nothing: this is how you search the filled part of a buffer and leave the rest alone.

You can search for more than a value. One overload takes an IComparable<T> — an object that compares itself with an element: the method calls comparable.CompareTo(element), and a positive result means “the target is to the right”. If the comparable is a struct, the generic overload BinarySearch<T, TComparable> kicks in, with no boxing.

In a game: snapshot interpolation in a networked game. The snapshot buffer is sorted by time, the frame is rendered slightly in the past — at renderTime — and you need the two snapshots around it. That is the insertion point: snapshot i is the first one later than renderTime, i − 1 is the last one not later.
cards/7/task: Search for 33 in [4, 9, 15, 21, 30, 42, 57, 63] — it is not there. Step through the trace; the rig will stop twice. Watch not mid, but what is known about the elements left of lo and right of hi.
cards/7/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: lo = 5, hi = 4: no candidates, the loop ends
cards/7/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: hi = 3: we keep looking for 33 to the left
cards/7/goal/asks/0/q: One candidate is left, [4..4], and a[4] = 30 < 33. What happens to the bounds?
cards/7/goal/asks/0/explain: 30 < 33 — so everything left of index 4 is less than 33 too: lo = mid + 1 = 5. Now lo > hi, and the invariant says there are no candidates. Proving that 33 is absent took three comparisons out of eight possible.
cards/7/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: lo = 5 is the insertion point of 33; Array.BinarySearch would return ~5 = −6
cards/7/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: lo means nothing: 33 is absent, and Array.BinarySearch returns −1
cards/7/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: The insertion point is hi = 4; Array.BinarySearch would return ~4 = −5
cards/7/goal/asks/1/q: The loop ends with lo = 5, hi = 4. What is true about lo?
cards/7/goal/asks/1/explain: When the closed variant exits, lo = hi + 1, and both halves of the invariant meet: a[0..4] = [4, 9, 15, 21, 30] are less than 33, a[5..7] = [42, 57, 63] are greater. So lo = 5 is the insertion point, and Array.BinarySearch encodes it as ~5 = −6. Index 4 is the last element less than 33, not the insertion point.
cards/8/q: LowerBound on [1, 3, 5]: with x = 4 it hangs, with x = 9 it throws IndexOutOfRangeException. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/8/explain: The bounds are half-open, but the loop condition belongs to the closed variant. With lo == hi the band is empty, yet the loop keeps going. If hi = n, then mid = n and a[mid] is past the end (x = 9). If hi < n, the branch else hi = mid changes nothing — an infinite loop (x = 4: lo = hi = 2). One convention for the whole solution: [lo, hi) and while (lo < hi).
cards/9/title: Variations: where else a boundary hides
cards/9/body:
First and last occurrence (LeetCode #34, in O(log n)). first = LowerBound(x); if first == n or a[first] != x, x is absent and the answer is [−1, −1]; otherwise last = UpperBound(x) − 1. Two searches are still O(log n). Finding x and expanding outwards is O(n) when x fills the whole array.
Where to insert (#35) is exactly lower_bound.
Closest to x: i = LowerBound(x), and the candidates are a[i − 1] and a[i], if they exist.

Peak (Find Peak Element, #162). The array is not sorted, neighbours differ, and beyond the edges there is −∞; return any element greater than both neighbours, in O(log n). If a[mid] < a[mid + 1], there is definitely a peak to the right of mid: the slope goes up, and at the edge there is −∞. So lo = mid + 1, otherwise hi = mid. Invariant: there is a peak in [lo..hi].

The takeaway: binary search does not need a sorted array, it needs a question about the middle whose answer splits the candidates into “definitely not here” and “definitely here”. That is what the rest of this unit is about.
cards/10/q: You are solving First and Last Position (#34) out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/10/items/0: Clarify: is the order non-decreasing? What to return if x is absent? Can the array be empty?
cards/10/items/1: Naive: find x and expand left and right — O(n) when x fills the whole array
cards/10/items/2: Idea: look for two boundaries, not an element — lower_bound and upper_bound
cards/10/items/3: Code with the invariant a[0..lo) < x ≤ a[hi..n) and the loop while (lo < hi)
cards/10/items/4: Run [5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10] with x = 8: boundaries 3 and 5, answer [3, 4]
cards/10/items/5: Complexity: two O(log n) searches, O(1) memory
cards/10/items/6: Edge cases: x absent, x below or above everything, an empty array
cards/10/explain: The same seven-step script. The example [5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10] checks both boundaries at once, and x = 6 on the same array checks the [−1, −1] branch: LowerBound returns 1, and there is a 7 there.
cards/11/title: How many iterations, and when you don’t need binary search
cards/11/body:
Each iteration keeps at most half of the candidates, so there are at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 iterations: 20 for 10⁶, 30 for 10⁹. But in real code constants matter too.

A small array. With a few dozen elements a linear scan is often no slower: it reads memory sequentially, and the CPU almost never mispredicts its branches. Measure the threshold, don’t guess it.
Many queries over unchanging data — sort once in O(n log n) and answer each query in O(log n). If the data changes often, a sorted array with Insert costs O(n) per insertion — then use SortedSet from the first unit.
cards/11/deep:
A proof in two parts. Correctness: the invariant holds at the start and every branch preserves it. Termination: hi − lo strictly decreases and cannot decrease forever. If you cannot name both parts, there is an off-by-one somewhere.

Inside .NET. Array.BinarySearch<T> and List<T>.BinarySearch are the closed variant: midpoint lo + ((hi − lo) >> 1), a three-way comparison, ~lo on exit. For Span the midpoint is computed as (int)(((uint)hi + (uint)lo) >> 1): the sum in uint cannot overflow because both numbers are non-negative and below 2³¹. The untyped overload Array.BinarySearch(Array, object) takes the value as object, so it gets boxed, and for arrays of non-primitive structs every element it reads is boxed too; when the array type is known, C# picks the generic one.

Branchless. The “left or right” jump is unpredictable, and on large arrays every misprediction costs on the order of 15–20 cycles. The “base and length” variant tracks the start and size of the band instead of lo and hi, and the base update is written as a conditional assignment that the compiler can emit without a jump. Faster still on big data is a layout in tree traversal order (Eytzinger): nodes probed one after another sit next to each other, so there are fewer cache misses. This is for hot paths; in an interview it is enough to name it.

Unity. In com.unity.collections, NativeArray, NativeList and UnsafeList have BinarySearch with the same convention: the index or the bitwise complement of the insertion point. Inside it is exactly the “base and length” variant, and it works in Burst. The Java idiom (lo + hi) >>> 1 does not compile in C# 9 — the >>> operator arrived in C# 11.
